blocks.text: That among the later Jews it was held almost a matter of religion to give idols and idol worship opprobrious names, among which זבול, dung, was a common one, Lightfoot has proved from the Talmudic writers in his Horae Hebraicae on Matth. XII, 25. But Michaelis, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. I, p. 205, and in the Notes on the vernacular version of Matth. X, 25, holds that Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul], which is read in the N. T., is altogether different from בעל זבוב, the god of the Ekronites, and not formed from it, but is to be explained from judicial astrology. "This," he says, "divides the heavens into 12 houses, setting one of the planets over each house, which in the terminology of that art is called the lord of the house. זבול is a dwelling, but above all a dwelling of the stars; properly, then, בעל זבול is a planet, the lord of a heavenly house, as Venus is of the house of Virgo. And since these planets were held to be gods by the heathen, who closely joined astrology with the worship of vain deities, and since the Jews held the gods of the nations to be evil demons, what was more natural than to call the prince of the demons (perhaps not the one prince of all, but yet the chief of some order, and more powerful than the rest) the lord of the heavenly house? Now the words of Christ will also become wonderfully clear, and will have a certain allusion and point: εἰ τον οἰκοδεσπότην [ei ton oikodespotēn] (רב הבית, or, as it is in the Hebrew gospel, בעל הבית) Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul] (בעל זבול) ἐκάλεσαν [ekalesan]." This opinion would not displease me either, provided Michaelis had proved by examples that the word זבול is used in astrology in the sense that he himself assigns to it.
